html:
The Samnite Wars were three wars fought between 343 and 290 BCE by the Roman Republic against the Samnites, a group of tough hill peoples of the southern Apennines. They decided who would rule central and southern Italy.

  • The First Samnite War (343 to 341 BCE) began when Rome answered a call for help from Capua in Campania.
  • The Second (326 to 304 BCE) was the longest. In 321 BCE a Roman army was trapped at the Caudine Forks and made to pass under a yoke of spears, a deep humiliation. Rome came back and won.
  • The Third (298 to 290 BCE) saw Samnites, Gauls, Etruscans and Umbrians join against Rome. Rome beat them together at Sentinum in 295 BCE.

The wars changed Rome. It adopted a more flexible army of small units called maniples, suited to hill fighting. It built the Appian Way to move troops south to Campania. It planted colonies of settlers across Italy. By 290 BCE Rome was the leading power in Italy, and its next rival was the Greek city of Tarentum, which brought on the Pyrrhic War.
